item.title: Panchan's Mining Island [Guest Diary], (Wed, Oct 14th)
item.description: [This is a Guest Diary by Zachary Norwood, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]
item.content:encoded:
[This is a Guest Diary by Zachary Norwood, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]

Crypto mining malware has been active and spreading across the internet for quite some time now. Moreover, the DShield honeypot picked up a worm that self-propagates through a plethora of means. One of them is stealing SSH keys after it gains access to a system. Furthermore, it also leverages a rootkit to maintain access to infected systems. One would hope that threat actors would have moved on past this worm by now. However, due to its rudimentary design and its effectiveness, they have had no reason to move on.

A malicious binary was uploaded and executed on the DShield honeypot, and that is where a copy of the Panchan worm was obtained. It is written with Golang, and it is a peer-to-peer botnet. Moreover, this worm was first identified in 2022. Many vendors recognize this worm now as seen below. 

VirusTotal

Clamscan

Therefore, a system with security controls such as egress filtering, ingress filtering, access control lists, continuous monitoring, and passwordless authentication will prevent this worm from taking root. However, many systems are insecure and unpatched. This is why this worm is still propagating across the internet. The strings captured from the binary below show how simple it is to find its command-and-control channel and the functions that it consists of.

Furthermore, leveraging something as simple as syslog to pull logs and using commands such as grep to find privilege escalation activities, software installation, software removal, and access to ports such as SSH will allow an analyst to identify this activity. However, this does not scale well. Therefore, leveraging a SIEM to gather and parse this data is a much more effective solution. Next, all traffic entering and exiting from both the trusted and untrusted networks needs to pass through at least one firewall. Preferably, also having an intrusion detection or prevention system right after the public facing firewall in the trusted zone.

 
Command and Control Channel

Panchan Functions

These captures clearly show the source files that the Panchan worm consists of. To dig deeper into what this binary can do, a network simulator was used. Moreover, the specific network simulator that was used was FakeNet-NG with Wireshark to intercept the network traffic. These tools were used to identify what URL it was reaching out to once it was installed on a system. FakeNet-NG is a tool developed by the Mandiant FLARE team for dynamic network analysis. This tool simulates legitimate network traffic, allowing an analyst to identify how the malware interacts with the network and if it is communicating with an external server. This specific strain of this worm was using a discord channel as a command-and-control server. This was identified by capturing and dissecting the network traffic that was generated by the worm interacting with the FakeNet-NG network. 

FAKENET-NG

Wireshark Capture

Panchan, the peer-to-peer crypto mining worm, is a threat to any organization who has internet facing servers. This worm is mainly a threat to insecure systems, and opening SSH to a public network needs to be done in a secure way. Fail2Ban is a service that scans log files for repeated failed login attempts. This service then blocks that IP address by updating the system’s firewall rule. Fail2Ban is another control that should be put in place with a public facing SSH port. Services like SSH should have multi-factor authentication, and an access control list. The access control list should include specific IP addresses or a jump box. Disabling root login with SSH is another essential security control that needs to be implemented.

With SSH, public and private key pairs are another option for authentication. This will then create the capability to disable password authentication for the SSH service preventing brute force attacks. However, these key pairs are often created and forgotten about. This is a security concern, and SSH private keys are something that this worm is designed to steal. Once it has stolen a private key, it attempts to pivot to hosts in the running user’s SSH known_hosts file. A simple mitigation to protect the data within the known_hosts file is to use the HashKnownHosts option within a systems SSH configuration. Furthermore, it is best to mitigate long lived credentials and SSH key stealing by leveraging tools likeHashiCorp Vault to sign SSH certificates with short expirations. This ensures that reusing a key becomes highly impractical or even impossible. The user will authenticate to Vault with their credentials then they send their SSH public key to Vault for signing, and finally Vault then signs the SSH key. Then it returns the SSH certificate to the user. This certificate can be used to log in to any host configured to trust the Vault CA. Leveraging such infrastructure will also allow an organization to disable password authentication entirely for services like SSH.

Furthermore, leveraging something as simple as syslog to pull logs and using commands such as grep to find privilege escalation activities, software installation, software removal, and access to ports such as SSH will allow an analyst to identify this activity. However, this does not scale well. Therefore, leveraging a SIEM to gather and parse this data is a much more effective solution. Next, all traffic entering and exiting from both the trusted and untrusted networks needs to pass through at least one firewall. Preferably, also having an intrusion detection or prevention system right after the public facing firewall in the trusted zone.

Typical indicators of compromise for this worm include multiple failed authentication attempts via SSH, unusual resource usage on infected systems, and processes that cannot be killed by any means. This worm also creates hidden directories in the running users home directory or folders like /tmp. Often, these directories have names that are strings that have high amounts of entropy. For this strain of this worm, servers reaching out to services like Discord on a regular basis is another indicator of compromise that an analyst can look for. In conclusion, denying by default and allowing by exception is a vital strategy for systems facing untrusted networks. These same techniques that were discussed above can be used to protect critical public facing infrastructure from threat actors. 

[1] https://github.com/mandiant/GoReSym
[2] https://github.com/mandiant/flare-fakenet-ng
[3] https://www.akamai.com/blog/security-research/new-p2p-botnet-panchan
[4] https://www.akamai.com/blog/security-research/cryptominer-anatomy-internals
[5] https://attack.mitre.org/
[6] https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/secrets/ssh/signed-ssh-certificates
[7] https://www.hashicorp.com/en/blog/managing-ssh-access-at-scale-with-hashicorp-vault
[8] https://github.com/bruneaug/DShield-SIEM/tree/main
[9] https://www.sans.edu/cyber-security-programs/bachelors-degree/

item.title: Measuring Human Cryptanalysis Effort
item.description:
Matthew Green has a new site that tries to estimate the number of cryptanalyst-hours that have been spent analyzing different public-key algorithms:

Abstract: We estimate how much public cryptanalysis each public-key assumption has received, using the literature itself as the instrument. From roughly sixteen thousand candidate papers we classify cryptanalytic work on ECDLP, structured and plain lattices, syndrome decoding and their comparators, then convert papers into estimated research-allocation years through a person-level author map. These publication-based estimates may substantially overstate actual time spent. Lattices have overtaken elliptic curves in this cumulative measure only recently; we express that history as inference budgets under stated productivity assumptions. The study was conducted by AI models: Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 built the pipeline, ran the analysis and wrote this page, with contributions from GPT-6 Astra. Matthew Green set the questions, made the key methodological decisions and oversaw the work...
item.content:encoded:
Matthew Green has a new site that tries to estimate the number of cryptanalyst-hours that have been spent analyzing different public-key algorithms:

Abstract: We estimate how much public cryptanalysis each public-key assumption has received, using the literature itself as the instrument. From roughly sixteen thousand candidate papers we classify cryptanalytic work on ECDLP, structured and plain lattices, syndrome decoding and their comparators, then convert papers into estimated research-allocation years through a person-level author map. These publication-based estimates may substantially overstate actual time spent. Lattices have overtaken elliptic curves in this cumulative measure only recently; we express that history as inference budgets under stated productivity assumptions. The study was conducted by AI models: Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 built the pipeline, ran the analysis and wrote this page, with contributions from GPT-6 Astra. Matthew Green set the questions, made the key methodological decisions and oversaw the work.

There are a lot of caveats to this analysis. It relies on published work, so anything unpublished does not count. This includes both academic cryptanalysis that didn’t result in a paper, and intelligence agency cryptanalysis done in secret. But it’s a good first stab at a metric of this sort.

item.title: Q3 2026 Cyber Attacks Statistics
item.description: In the third quarter of 2026, I recorded 588 cyber incidents. Cyber Crime accounted for 77.1% of motivations, Malware was the most common attack technique at 31.9%, and Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190) led initial access at 30.4%. Information and Communication was the hardest-hit sector.

item.title: ‘Nightmare Scenario’: Zero-Click Spyware Is Infecting Phones via Targeted Ads
item.description: Researchers at The Citizen Lab have for the first time released technical evidence of sophisticated mercenary spyware being distributed via online advertising.

item.title: Google and Singapore Develop AI Scam Detector That Works Entirely on Your Phone

item.title: The Future of AI Cryptanalysis
item.description:
Matthew Green has been writing a rather pessimistic series of posts about the potential for AI systems to vastly outperform humans in cryptanalysis of both symmetric and public-key ciphers.

I am more optimistic than he is. That is, I have stronger faith in the over-engineering cryptographers tend to do. I am trying to write this up in more detail.

item.title: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
item.description: The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
item.content:encoded:
The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”

The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.

Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

item.title: Cyberattack on Connected Fridges in France
item.description:
Another IoT cyberattack, this one in France:

Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight, according to one supermarket chain affected.

[…]

Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot, although Danfoss did not confirm any reports about just how warm the fridges and freezers could become in that process.

Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified...
item.content:encoded:
Another IoT cyberattack, this one in France:

Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight, according to one supermarket chain affected.

[…]

Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot, although Danfoss did not confirm any reports about just how warm the fridges and freezers could become in that process.

Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified.

Any IoT device that can’t be updated is vulnerable. And, probably, any IoT device that can be updated is also vulnerable.

item.title: The hidden network: Inside the phishing infrastructure ecosystem powering global cybercrime
item.description:
Microsoft uncovered a Chinese-language cybercriminal ecosystem, an interconnected network of phishing kit operators (tracked as Storm-2990), and an illicit marketplace (tracked as Storm-3119) selling tools and infrastructure for large-scale phishing. In collaboration with law enforcement agencies and other partners worldwide, Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit (DCU) facilitated a disruption of the ecosystem.

The post The hidden network: Inside the phishing infrastructure ecosystem powering global cybercrime appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
item.content:encoded:
1. Uncovering the shadow world of a phishing kit ecosystem
  2. Storm-3119: YAM Store, the power broker
  3. Storm-2990: The Iron Man System phishing kit
  4. Downstream activity from Storm-2990 phishing kits
  5. Mitigation and protection guidance
  6. Microsoft Defender detections

Over the past year, Microsoft uncovered a Chinese-language cybercriminal ecosystem, an interconnected network of phishing kit operators, developers, and an illicit marketplace selling tools and infrastructure for large-scale phishing, enabling cybercriminal operations worldwide.

Threat actors purchased and used these tools and infrastructure, including phishing kits and access to compromised or fraudulent Microsoft or Google cloud environments and related credentials, to target organizations across the healthcare, financial services, wholesale distribution, and information technology (IT) sectors in Japan, the United States, Australia, and India. In collaboration with law enforcement agencies and other partners worldwide, Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit (DCU) facilitated a disruption of the ecosystem’s primary developers and infrastructure.

Microsoft’s research into one phishing kit unraveled a larger ecosystem, including the phishing kit developers, an infrastructure dealer, and the threat actors who buy from both. In this blog, we examine several phishing kits marketed and sold through YAM Store, an underground marketplace tracked by Microsoft as Storm-3119. We share our analysis of the technical aspects of this Chinese-language phishing kit ecosystem, the shared infrastructure, provisioning methods, and downstream activity by threat actors using these tools.

Uncovering the shadow world of a phishing kit ecosystem

Microsoft, alongside industry partner Resecurity, identified three phishing kits sold through the YAM Store that make up this Chinese-language cybercriminal network: CoGUI (also known as NX or FA), Haozi (also known as Phoenix), and Iron Man System. Microsoft tracks the cluster of activity and the developers behind all three phishing kits as Storm-2990. Since January 2026, the threat actors behind these kits have been responsible for facilitating the sending of over one billion phishing emails and SMS messages to over 75 thousand organizations worldwide.

Microsoft assesses with high confidence that these phishing kits were developed by Chinese-speaking threat actors, and, despite their distinct branding and separate Telegram-based sales channels, exhibit highly similar capabilities and functionality. The phishing kits provide phishing templates impersonating legitimate brands and organizations (including government, financial, and logistics) worldwide, and enable criminal actors to facilitate high-volume phishing and credential stealing operations. The similarity in their infrastructure and overlap in activity suggest either shared development origins, code reuse, or close collaboration among their developers.

These phishing kits have been advertised through YAM Store, first CoGUI and Haozi, followed by Iron Man System starting in June 2026. YAM Store and affiliated phishing kit companies accepted payments through cryptocurrency, including USDT and Ethereum, adding another layer to conceal illicit activity. The scale and proliferation of this ecosystem demonstrate how readily available criminal infrastructure can lower the barrier to entry, enabling less skilled cybercriminals to target organizations at scale and contribute to fraud losses.

By mapping the relationship between YAM Store and these phishing kits, we provide insight into the commercial infrastructure that supports modern phishing operations.

Storm-3119: YAM Store, the power broker

YAM Store is an initial access broker (IAB) that sells infrastructure using compromised or fraudulently obtained environments in providers like Microsoft and Google. The marketplace offers a variety of infrastructure based on age, subscription type, and environment types such as education (.edu) or non-profit (.org).

The YAM Store marketplace provides cybercriminals with a platform to purchase fraudulently acquired Microsoft and Google domains associated with legitimate, expired, or previously used organization numbers, allowing actors to use seemingly legitimate infrastructure and obtain workspaces at relatively low cost. Storm-3119 uses automation to identify expired environment or organization names and leverages legitimate customer information associated with them to help circumvent existing detections.

Anatomy of YAM Store operations: How Storm-3119 acquires, controls, and monetizes infrastructure

During this investigation, Microsoft uncovered a five-stage attack pipeline often used in Storm-3119’s operations. YAM Store functions as an access broker, an intermediary that hijacks Microsoft 365 and Azure for Education tenants and resells the stolen accounts, licenses, and storage as a service to downstream operations, including the phishing kits tracked as Storm-2990. The pipeline below describes the supply side of that business: how the actor acquires, controls, and monetizes compromised environments.

Stage 1 – Reconnaissance: Storm-3119 conducts automated reconnaissance of target environments. The actor uses Flask, a lightweight Python web framework, to covertly identify and profile cloud-enabled organizations. The tooling is designed to discover Microsoft 365 tenants, assess enrollment opportunities, gather licensing and Azure cloud information, and perform these activities anonymously through Tor infrastructure.

Stage 2 – Environment takeover and app-only admin panels: Once a viable environment is identified, the threat actor centralizes associated information in an actor-controlled platform used to administer compromised Microsoft 365 environments. This platform is a separate set of administrative panels (implemented in PHP, Java/Spring, and Cloudflare Workers) that lets the operator maintain, monetize, and expand access using stolen application credentials. Leveraging the compromised environment’s client secret through an application-only authentication flow, the panel performs full directory control: it resets passwords silently (without forcing a change at next sign-in), assigns education licenses, and grants privileged attributes that the actor can later monetize. Because this access is application-level rather than tied to a single user session, the resulting persistence is more durable, more scalable, and harder to detect.

Stage 3 – Storage and resource abuse: With the stolen privileged credentials, the threat actor signs in to a compromised Global Administrator account and self-provisions the PnP Management Shell service principal, which represents the actor’s application inside the compromised tenant. Through this service principal, the threat actor grants themselves broad Microsoft Graph permissions, including read and write access to directory data and AppCatalog.ReadWrite.All, along with full control over the SharePoint API. The actor then abuses the compromised tenant’s SharePoint and OneDrive as bulk hosting and converts the hijacked storage into a sellable product.

Stage 4 – Phishing and DNS infrastructure support: The threat actor maintains dedicated infrastructure to support and manage phishing operations on behalf of their customers. A custom DNS management platform enables centralized control of phishing domains, SSL certificates, and domain-routing configurations through Cloudflare.

Stage 5 – Storefront and monetization: Storm-3119 resells the hijacked accounts, licenses, and storage through an automated storefront, operating as the access broker that supplies these resources to downstream operations. Payment is accepted through Alipay, WeChat Pay, and USDT (TRC20), and the storefront supports a sub-reseller tier. Telegram is used for order notifications and buyer contact rather than as the primary sales channel.

In addition to targeting existing tenants, Storm-3119 also separately creates fraudulent organizations and supporting web presence to establish tenants on Microsoft’s platform, likely using AI-generated content and forged documentation to make the fabricated entities appear legitimate. In one case, the actor created an environment, likely using AI, named “Jewish Choice” under the guise of a nonprofit organization and associated it with jewishchoice[.]org, a domain registered only within the past several months that did not appear to represent a legitimate organization. This activity indicates that Storm-3119 likely established the website and associated domain to lend credibility to the fabricated nonprofit identity and facilitate tenant creation.

Storm-2990: The Iron Man System phishing kit

YAM Store sells its illicitly acquired infrastructure, as well as the prominent phishing kits tracked as Storm-2990, to other threat actors. The platforms are commercially licensed phishing-as-a-service (PaaS) products. They are designed to impersonate organizations across several industry verticals to steal information, including sign-in credentials (usernames, passwords) and financial data (credit card information), used to gain access to network environments.

Iron Man System’s customers purchase a subscription that provides access to the kit’s license server, with the domain hard-coded into the kit. This restriction adds a layer of obfuscation by limiting site access to paying customers. The kits allow attackers to steal money by abusing the stolen credit card information.

The Iron Man System phishing kit contains over 2,335 templates tailored to over 139 countries including Australia, Japan, India, and the United States, with the United States accounting for the most phishing templates. The phishing lures used by Iron Man System mimic various trusted brands and organizations, such as local government including authorities associated with traffic and parking fees, law enforcement, healthcare, finance, transportation, and retail. These lures are designed to trick targets into providing sensitive information. Most phishing lures used in the United States are transportation or government-related.

The phishing kits are capable of the following advanced evasion techniques to varying degrees:

  • Geofencing, a technique used to restrict access to configured countries only, so only users from specific countries can access the phishing content from their web browser
  • Fake CAPTCHA gates, used to prevent or block automated browsing from threat research tools by making the user click a box or execute an action
  • IP address block list and allow list, used to block or allow IP addresses to prevent threat researcher interaction
  • Anti-detection configuration related tosettings to evade security researcher detection
  • Telegram bot configuration,including bot tokens and chat IDs for real-time phishing that enables credential exfiltration. It allows the kit operator to receive automatic notifications on their Telegram account when a target takes action on a phishing lure, including entering credentials, credit card data submission, and verification codes.

After the target provides the sensitive information (sign-in details, credit card info), the phishing kit collects it using a WebSocket, offering customers real-time victim interaction through Telegram notifications during credential harvesting. This confirms that the kit supports live, interactive phishing where the operator monitors each victim’s progress and manually controls what the victim sees next, a hallmark of sophisticated PaaS platforms. The attacker then harvests the information to use in follow-on fraudulent financial activities.

The Iron Man System phishing kit panel is predominately hosted on China-based hosting providers, with a smaller number of panels found on hosting providers in other countries. The fully featured, multi-tenant phishing kit uses the GoFrame application development framework, an open-source Go framework with roots in the Chinese developer ecosystem.

Downstream activity from Storm-2990 phishing kits

Microsoft observed downstream activity by threat actors using infrastructure affiliated with the Storm-2990 phishing kits. In analyzed cases, the actors used similar common phishing techniques, such as urgency in the message and attaching malicious links that redirect to actor-controlled infrastructure that allows these downstream threat actors to perform the following activities:

  • Credential stealing: The actors use phishing pages that impersonate legitimate services to trick targets into providing credentials or other authentication information, enabling downstream actors to access compromised accounts.
  • Device code phishing: In some cases, the actors abuse the device code authentication flow to trick victims into authenticating to legitimate applications, allowing downstream actors to obtain authentication tokens and access compromised accounts.
  • Financial fraud: The end goal for the downstream actors is to use stolen payment data to make fraudulent purchases of high-end goods or fraudulent transactions on legitimate financial platforms.

The threat actors using the phishing kits conduct phishing campaigns at scale whether it is a missing toll payment or a traffic citation. The following screenshots show email or SMS phishing lures used in Storm-2990 phishing kits.

Mitigation and protection guidance

This interconnected network of Chinese-language phishing kit operators and developers operates as an enabling ecosystem, providing infrastructure and services that facilitate criminal activity rather than functioning as a standalone malware tool. Microsoft assesses that the ecosystem is not limited to the abuse of Microsoft services and extends to other providers.

While Microsoft notes that the identified organizations impacted by attacks stemming from Storm-3119 or Storm-2990 operations include financial, healthcare, and IT companies, the activity conducted by threat actors using these tools are common attacks that could affect any organization.

Most of the activity that stems from this phishing kit ecosystem consists of social engineering, phishing operations, and account and storage takeovers. Microsoft recommends the following to mitigate the impact of Storm-3119 and Storm-2990-related threats.

  • In nearly all the cases observed by Microsoft, the phishing lures used by the Storm-2990 operators followed prescriptive scam red flags, including urgency, time-sensitive tasks such as clicking a provided link with official branding. Users should verify with the purported sender of the message or email, even when the task involves signing in to a known, secure account not provided by the link or calling the purported organization or company directly.
  • Educate users about protecting personal and business information in social media, filtering unsolicited communication, identifying lures in spear-phishing emails and watering holes, and reporting reconnaissance attempts and other suspicious activities.
  • Educate users about common phishing techniques. Sign-in prompts should clearly identify the application being authenticated to. As of 2021, Microsoft Azure interactions prompt the user to confirm (Cancel or Continue) that they are signing in to the app they expect, which is an option frequently missing from phishing sign-ins.
  • Review our recommended settings for Exchange Online Protection and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to ensure your organization has established essential defenses and knows how to monitor and respond to threat activity.
  • Configure the Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Links policy to apply to internal recipients.

Hardening credentials and cloud identities is also necessary to defend against phishing attacks, which seek to gain valid credentials and access tokens. As an initial step, use passwordless solutions like passkeys and implement multifactor authentication (MFA) throughout your environment:

  • Invoke the principles of least privilege and Zero Trust to significantly slow down threat actors who might have been able to gain initial access and buy time for defenders to respond. Since Storm-3119 operators have been observed obtaining Global Administrator access, implementing these principles can help lock down Global Administrator roles and who has access to specific resources.
  • Use the Microsoft Authenticator app for passkeys and MFA, and complement MFA with Conditional Access policies, where sign-in requests are evaluated using additional identity-driven signals.
  • Conditional Access policies can also be scoped to strengthen privileged accounts with phishing-resistant MFA.
  • Your passkey and MFA policy can be further secured by only allowing MFA and passkey registrations from trusted locations and devices.
  • Enable network protection to prevent applications or users from accessing malicious domains and other malicious content on the internet.

Microsoft Defender detections

Microsoft Defender customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below. Microsoft Defender coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog.

The coverage below applies to the downstream activity detected by Microsoft that was identified using Storm-2990 infrastructure.

Microsoft Security Copilot

Microsoft Security Copilot is embedded in Microsoft Defender and provides security teams with AI-powered capabilities to summarize incidents, analyze files and scripts, summarize identities, use guided responses, and generate device summaries, hunting queries, and incident reports.

Customers can also deploy AI agents, including the following Microsoft Security Copilot agents, to perform security tasks efficiently:

  • Threat Intelligence Briefing agent
  • Phishing Triage agent
  • Threat Hunting agent
  • Dynamic Threat Detection agent

Security Copilot is also available as a standalone experience where customers can perform specific security-related tasks, such as incident investigation, user analysis, and vulnerability impact assessment. In addition, Security Copilot offers developer scenarios that allow customers to build, test, publish, and integrate AI agents and plugins to meet unique security needs.

Threat intelligence reports

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use the following threat analytics reports in the Defender portal (requires license for at least one Defender XDR product) to get the most up-to-date information about the activity and techniques discussed in this blog. These reports provide intelligence, protection information, and recommended actions to prevent, mitigate, or respond to associated threats found in customer environments.

  • Threat Overview Profile: Evolving phishing threats

Microsoft Security Copilot customers can also use the Microsoft Security Copilot integration in Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence, either in the Security Copilot standalone portal or in the embedded experience in the Microsoft Defender portal to get more information about the activity discussed in this blog.

References

  • CoGUI Phish Kit Targets Japan with Millions of Messages | Proofpoint US
  • IronToll: Global Government-Impersonation PhaaS | PhishEye

Learn more

For the latest security research from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community, check out the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Blog.

To get notified about new publications and to join discussions on social media, follow us on LinkedIn, X (formerly Twitter), and Bluesky.

To hear stories and insights from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community about the ever-evolving threat landscape, listen to the Microsoft Threat Intelligence podcast.

The post The hidden network: Inside the phishing infrastructure ecosystem powering global cybercrime appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.

item.title: TruConfidence: Why Your Patch Automation Can Finally Be Autonomous
item.description: TruConfidence: The AI-Powered Remediation Intelligence & Orchestration engine powering TruRisk Eliminate 2.0 delivers autonomous remediation at scale with proof at every step. Executive Summary Vulnerabilities are now discovered faster than enterprises can remediate them. Patch automation has been around for years, but vulnerability backlogs are still growing. Automation isn’t the bottleneck. Confidence is: without evidence […]
item.content:encoded:
TruConfidence: The AI-Powered Remediation Intelligence & Orchestration engine powering TruRisk Eliminate 2.0 delivers autonomous remediation at scale with proof at every step.

Executive Summary

Vulnerabilities are now discovered faster than enterprises can remediate them. Patch automation has been around for years, but vulnerability backlogs are still growing. Automation isn’t the bottleneck. Confidence is: without evidence of how a change will behave, Security and IT teams hold back, and the backlog grows. TruRisk Eliminate 2.0, the Autonomous RemOps platform, closes that confidence gap. TruConfidence, its remediation and orchestration intelligence engine, determines the safest, most effective way to eliminate each validated exposure while Agent Sara, Qualys’ risk remediation AI agent, executes these plans in customer-defined waves and progressive rings. Scanner-based remediation reaches edge and perimeter devices with the same Qualys scanners. Every change is monitored for operational health, rolled back automatically if anomalies arise, and closed with evidence. This approach enables rapid remediation without risking business continuity. In the past year, Qualys has deployed 178 million patches, with 40 million fully autonomous and a rollback rate under 0.1%.

Patch automation has existed for years. Yet in most enterprises, automated remediation jobs still wait in line behind change approvals and maintenance windows while critical exposures stay open.

The reason is that risk cuts both ways. Leave a vulnerability unpatched, and you invite exploitation. Push a faulty update, and you risk failed installs, rollbacks, or outages.  Without evidence of how a change will behave, Security and IT teams default to caution, and the backlog grows.

Patch automation was never the blocker. Confidence is.

Today, we’re closing this gap with TruRisk Eliminate 2.0, the Autonomous RemOps platform. Powered by TruConfidence, its AI-powered Remediation and Orchestration Intelligence engine, and Agent Sara, Qualys’ autonomous AI agent for risk remediation, TruRisk Eliminate determines the right remediation action and executes it across your entire attack surface while keeping operations resilient.

The Confidence Gap: Why the Remediation Backlog Keeps Growing

AI-powered discovery is finding vulnerabilities faster than ticket-driven remediation can close them. Patch Tuesday recently hit 974 CVEs in a single month, on a process built for about 100. Attackers are taking advantage. The Verizon 2026 DBIR found that 31% of breaches began with the exploitation of vulnerabilities, up from 20%, making it the top initial access vector.

Remediation has not kept pace. The same report shows the median time to remediate a known exploited vulnerability (KEV) rose from 32 to 43 days, and only 26% of KEVs are fully remediated. Qualys research shows the same widening gap between the speed of threats and the speed of remediation.

The ability to automate is not the constraint. Qualys customers already automate remediation at scale: automated patch deployments rose 81% between the first and second quarters of 2026. They can because Qualys gives them the evidence to trust each change, from which exposures matter to how reliably a patch will deploy. What stalls machine-speed remediation is the lack of evidence needed to confidently move beyond manual, human-led remediation workflows. Without that, automated or autonomous remediation stalls.

Before letting autonomous remediation run, Security and IT teams need answers to these questions:

  • What must be fixed? Only 1% of vulnerabilities are exploited in the wild. Teams need to fix the validated exposures first, then tackle the long tail.
  • Does it need a patch? Not every exposure needs one. A mitigation, an uninstall or an existing security control can close it faster, with less disruption. 
  • If it needs a patch, will it work and can it be automated? Teams need to predict whether a patch is safe to deploy and will not cause any business disruption, then roll it out progressively. 
  • How do we control the rollout?  Teams need to deploy changes progressively: zero-touch automation for high-reliability patches on low-impact applications, and ring-based deployment for everything else.
  • Did the environment stay healthy? Teams need ensure that risk was eliminated to maintain operational resiliency.

Answer these four questions with evidence, and remediation can run at machine speed without putting business continuity at risk. 

How it Fits in the Autonomous RemOps Cycle

Closing that gap takes more than a better patch tool. It takes a new operating model for remediation: Autonomous RemOps. 

Traditional patch tools push what is in the catalog and stop at “deployed.” Autonomous RemOps replaces that ticket-driven process with a continuous, evidence-based Decide → Execute → Prove.  It determines what to fix, executes the appropriate remediation path across the entire attack surface, and demonstrates that the business remained resilient.

TruRisk Eliminate 2.0 runs that cycle in five steps. First, Qualys ETM and Agent Val validate what must be fixed. Second, TruConfirm credits the controls already in place. TruConfidence powers the final three steps, where autonomy carries the most operational risk: choosing the remediation path, controlling the rollout, and proving that it held.

Meet TruConfidence: Remediation Intelligence You Can Trust

TruConfidence is the remediation and orchestration intelligence layer behind TruRisk Eliminate. For every exposure, it answers one question: what is the safest and most effective way to eliminate this risk? Agent Sara puts that answer to work through waves. Together, they cover the full remediation lifecycle before, during, and after every deployment.

TruConfidence Before the Deployment 

Once Qualys ETM and Agent Val have validated which exposures are exploitable and TruConfirm has credited the controls already in place, TruConfidence determines the right remediation path for each exposure.

Then you can determine whether a patch is needed at all. Patchless Remediation closes exposures by mitigating, uninstalling unused software, running a custom script or isolating the host. Third-Party Mitigation Intelligence extends those options through the tools teams already run, such as Zscaler and CrowdStrike. 

When a patch is the right remediation action, the AI-Powered Patch Reliability Scoring predicts whether the patch is safe to deploy before it runs, drawing on global telemetry and Qualys customer deployments. 

TruConfidence During the Rollout

Agent Sara efficiently implements TruConfidence’s decisions, eliminating ticket queues. She prioritizes eliminating the exploited 1% first and then automatically addresses the remaining vulnerabilities.

She organizes the backlog into remediation waves; each matched to its level of risk. You define the waves to fit your environment, and Agent Sara runs them. 

A typical setup might look like this:

  • Easy Fixes: High-reliability patches on low-impact assets deploy zero-touch.
  • Connectivity-Sensitive: Changes are sequenced carefully to protect systems with critical network dependencies. 
  • Operational Risk: Changes are held for closer review before proceeding.
  • Beyond Patching: Exposures are routed to the patchless path TruConfidence selected.

Every change moves through progressive rings, from Pilot to broad deployment, and is observed before it reaches the next tier. A low-reliability signal automatically pauses progression, keeping the blast radius as small as possible.

Agent Sara works within your rules, not around them, enforcing maintenance windows, asset groupings, and rollback controls, and requires human approval wherever a critical service, identity infrastructure, or production databases are involved.

TruConfidence After the Rollout 

A successful install is not the finish line. Operational Resiliency continues to correlate health signals after each change, monitoring for CPU spikes, memory issues, and service impact. Stable metrics confirm the change held, while anomalies pause the rollout and trigger rollback. When a remediation fails, AI-Powered Failure Analysis explains the root cause in plain language, such as a pending reboot or a missing prerequisite, and recommends the corrective action. Every change ends with evidence, which means faster recovery and fewer war rooms.

Remediation that reaches every corner of your attack surface

TruRisk Eliminate 2.0 goes past agent-based endpoints. It extends remediation to perimeter devices, cloud and applications, so teams can deal with an exposure wherever it lives. Each asset gets the response that fits it: patch it, mitigate the risk when no patch exists yet, uninstall the vulnerable software, isolate the asset or apply a custom fix.

For assets that can’t host an agent, Eliminate works through Qualys scanners and the security and IT integrations you already have. Every exposure gets a path to remediation, not just the ones on managed endpoints.

Proven in Production. Built to Keep Going

TruRisk Eliminate already runs remediation at scale:

Each pass through the cycle first closes validated exposures and moves the long tail into the next waves, so the backlog shrinks continuously rather than piling up between change windows. And because every change is backed by proof, TruRisk Eliminate becomes both the system of record and the system of action for cyber risk reduction.

Give your board confidence in security and business continuity.

Start a TruConfidence trial and watch TruRisk Eliminate 2.0 decide, execute, and prove remediation in your own environment.

item.title: Orphaned VBA Projects Inside DWG Files, (Wed, Oct 14th)
item.description: Years ago I wrote diary entries about VBA code stored inside AutoCAD drawing files (.dwg).
item.content:encoded:
Years ago I wrote diary entries about VBA code stored inside AutoCAD drawing files (.dwg).

In a nutshell: the VBA code is stored inside an OLE file, that is embedded inside the DWG file. You can do a brute-force search for the embedded OLE file, or you can follow a pointer inside the header of the DWG file.

I wrote a small Python script (autocad.py) for this second case. It looks at a 32-bit pointer at position 0x24 inside the DWG file. This points to a 16-byte long header, followed by the embedded file. This 16-byte long header contains the length of the embedded file. You use the script together with my tool cut-bytes.py, like this:

cut-bytes.py -S autocad.py -P AutoCAD : 461ed52aeb75384133a8238b2eb481ae5d505d4961effa622673d65a889c8218.vir.zip | oledump.py

 

This command carves the DWG file (inside the ZIP file) and extracts the embedded OLE file, and pipes it into oledump.py for analysis.

When the pointer is zero, there is no embedded OLE file, and cut-bytes.py returns nothing.

Recently, I discovered 2 DWG files that are an exception: their pointer to the embedded OLE file is zero, but if you do a brute-force search, you will find an embedded OLE file with a VBA project.

For example this DWG file.

Its pointer to the embedded VBA project is zero:

But it contains an embedded OLE file:

And right in front of the embedded OLE file, there is the 16-byte long header that contains the lenght of the embedded file.

Using the AutoCAD script to extract the file gives nothing:

But oledump.py can find the embedded OLE file and analyze it:

So while using oledump.py to analyze DWG files you find a VBA project embedded inside a DWG file, then also verify if it is not orphaned: verify that the pointer at 0x24 is not zero (or use the autocad.py script).

Because when a DWG file contains an orphaned VBA project, the VBA code can not have executed when someone opened the DWG file with AutoCAD. AutoCAD "does not see" orphaned VBA projects.

Notice that a default installation of AutoCAD does not support VBA. VBA for AutoCAD is a separate install.

I don't know how orphaning happens, but I did find an AutoLISP command to remove a VBA project from a DWG file: 

(dictremove (namedobjdict) "ACAD_VBA")

Maybe this dictremove command clears the pointer, but does not remove the embedded OLE file.

 

Didier Stevens
Senior handler
blog.DidierStevens.com

item.title: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
item.description: Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today's epic patch batch dwarfs September's record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

item.title: Microsoft Patch Tuesday, October 2026 Security Update Review
item.description: Microsoft has released its October 2026 Patch Tuesday security updates, addressing vulnerabilities across its products and services. As organizations continue to navigate an evolving threat landscape, applying security patches promptly remains critical to reducing exposure and strengthening security posture. This month’s updates highlight the importance of identifying affected assets, prioritizing remediation, and staying ahead of […]
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft has released its October 2026 Patch Tuesday security updates, addressing vulnerabilities across its products and services. As organizations continue to navigate an evolving threat landscape, applying security patches promptly remains critical to reducing exposure and strengthening security posture. This month’s updates highlight the importance of identifying affected assets, prioritizing remediation, and staying ahead of emerging risks. 

This Patch Tuesday is Microsoft’s largest security update ever, marking a significant increase over other recent massive releases, including the 400 security fixes in August and over 970 in September.

This month’s release addresses 1414 vulnerabilities, including 78 critical and 1329 important-severity vulnerabilities. 

In this month’s updates, Microsoft has addressed two vulnerabilities, one of which has been exploited in the wild. 

This month’s release includes fixes for several vulnerabilities that could potentially enable remote code execution, privilege escalation, or denial-of-service attacks. As always, timely patch deployment is crucial to reduce exposure and ensure systems remain resilient against exploitation attempts. 

InstaScan delivers detections within 60 minutes. After October’s Patch Tuesday, Agent Insta customers had them within 5 minutes.

Find out more about InstaScan

The October 2026 Microsoft vulnerabilities are classified as follows:

Adobe Patch for October 2026 

Adobe has released 11 advisories addressing 176 vulnerabilities across Adobe Experience Manager, Adobe ColdFusion, Adobe Commerce, Content Credentials SDK, Adobe Dimension, Adobe Photoshop, Adobe Substance 3D Stager, Adobe FrameMaker, Adobe Substance 3D Designer, Adobe Substance 3D Sampler, and Adobe Bridge. 23 of these vulnerabilities are rated critical. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities may lead to privilege escalation, arbitrary code execution, and bypassing security features.

Zero-day Vulnerabilities Patched in September Patch Tuesday Edition 

CVE-2026-96951: Windows Shell Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability 

A command injection flaw in Windows Shell may allow an unauthenticated attacker to bypass a security feature over a network. 

CISA added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog, acknowledging its active exploitation. CISA urged users to patch the vulnerability before October 16, 2026. 

CVE-2026-108398: .NET Framework Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability

An untrusted search path flaw in the .NET Framework may allow an authenticated attacker to bypass a security feature locally. 

Critical Severity Vulnerabilities Patched in September Patch Tuesday Edition

Microsoft Office PowerPoint Critical Vulnerabilities 

Microsoft Office Outlook Critical Vulnerabilities 

Microsoft Office Visio Critical Vulnerabilities 

Windows DHCP Server Critical Vulnerabilities 

Microsoft PostScript Printer Driver Critical Vulnerabilities 

Microsoft Office Word Critical Vulnerabilities 

Windows Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) Enclave Critical Vulnerabilities

Microsoft Office Excel Critical Vulnerabilities 

Other Microsoft Vulnerability Highlights

Microsoft Release Summary

This month’s security updates cover the following Microsoft product families:

Discover and Prioritize Vulnerabilities in Vulnerability Management, Detection & Response (VMDR)

Qualys VMDR automatically detects new Patch Tuesday vulnerabilities using continuous updates to its Knowledgebase (KB).

You can see all your impacted hosts by these vulnerabilities using the following QQL query:

Rapid Response with TruRisk Eliminate

Patch to the Latest Version

VMDR rapidly remediates Windows hosts by deploying the most relevant and applicable per-technology version patches. You can simply select the respective QIDs in the Patch Catalog and filter for “Missing” patches to identify and deploy the applicable, available patches with one click.

The following QQL will return the missing patches for this Patch Tuesday:

( qid: 110538 or qid: 110539 or qid: 388977 or qid: 388978 or qid: 50152 or qid: 92473 or qid: 92474 or qid: 92475 or qid: 92476 or qid: 92477 or qid: 92478 or qid: 92479 or qid: 92480 or qid: 92481 or qid: 92482 or qid: 92483 or qid: 92484 or qid: 92485 or qid: 92486 or qid: 92487 or qid: 92488 or qid: 92489 or qid: 92490 or qid: 92491 or qid: 92492 or qid: 92493 or qid: 92494 or qid: 92495 )
